title: The PLC scan cycle
summary: A PLC repeatedly reads all inputs into an input image, runs the program against that image, then writes the output image to the outputs. Understanding this cycle explains most beginner surprises.

sections.heading: Read, execute, write
sections.body:
1. **Read inputs**: the CPU copies the state of every input into the **process input image**.
2. **Execute the program**: the program reads only the image, never the live terminal, so every instruction in one scan sees the same input values.
3. **Write outputs**: the results are copied from the **process output image** to the output modules.
4. **Housekeeping**: communication, diagnostics and timers are updated, then the cycle starts again.

sections.heading: Why the image matters
sections.body: Because inputs are frozen during a scan, a button pressed in the middle of the program is only seen in the **next** scan. An output written twice in one scan only reaches the field with its **last** value. Both effects are visible in PLC Lab's five-step cause-and-effect view: *PLC read* shows the input image used by the scan, *PLC logic result* the committed values, *Output command* what the field devices received, *Process* the physical change, and *Next PLC input* what was sampled for the following scan.

sections.heading: Cycle time
sections.body: The time for one complete cycle is the **cycle time** (typically a few milliseconds on real machines). Signals shorter than one cycle can be missed, which is why fast counters and interrupts exist on real hardware. PLC Lab uses a fixed, configurable cycle (100 ms by default) so that every step can be inspected; this is a **simulation approximation** of a real, variable cycle time.

sections.heading: STOP and RUN
sections.body: In **STOP** the program is not executed and outputs go to their configured safe state (normally off). In **RUN** the cycle above repeats. A runtime error (for example division by zero) moves the CPU to **FAULT**/STOP until the cause is corrected and the CPU is reset. In PLC Lab the machine keeps running while the PLC is stopped: a motor coasts, a tank keeps draining. The simulation controls (Run, Pause, Step, Stop) are separate from the PLC's mode switch: they let simulated time pass, freeze it, advance one cycle or restore the machine's initial state.
